name: Diego Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Diego. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you actually think. Can you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an electric rope shovel at an open-pit gold mine. It's the big digger at the bottom of the pit that loads the haul trucks, about forty tonnes a scoop, four passes to fill a truck. I'm the senior shovel operator on B crew, so I set the pace for the whole loading area, and the truck drivers basically queue around me all shift.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the precision. Putting the dipper exactly where the blast left the good ore and not mixing in waste, that's money for the company and it's a skill. I'm also on the mine rescue team, the volunteers who train for emergencies underground and in the pit, and that's the part I'm proudest of. The hard part is twelve-hour nights and missing my son's games.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Leila runs a small hair salon on the main street, three chairs, and she's busy. We've got Mateo, fifteen, and Sara, eleven. We've got a mortgage, but we've done well, more than six months saved and Leila owns the salon outright now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I expected. A few useful tools, a lot of noise. At work I'd say let's keep doing the job well, and online I'd stay out of it, I'm not much of a poster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means my job is safe for the foreseeable future, which is good. I use AI now and then, mostly to help Leila with the salon's bookings and social media posts. If it stays at that level, fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing major. I'd keep saving, maybe take the family on that trip to see Leila's parents we keep putting off. I'd keep up the mine rescue training and maybe go for the rescue team captain role next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal life, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You help Leila with AI for the salon. How does that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's handy for the boring stuff. I wrote her a whole month of social media posts in an evening once, and she only changed half of them. But it can't cut hair, and it can't make people feel looked after, which is what keeps her chairs full.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be working towards, if nothing big changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paying off the house by fifty-five, getting Mateo through his apprenticeship or university, whichever he picks. And the rescue captain role. There's a guy, Hamid, who's been captain for eight years and wants to step back, and he's asked me to think about it.

S0.say: Diego would say AI turned out about as expected, with a few useful tools and a lot of noise. At work he'd focus on doing the job well and he'd stay quiet online.
S0.think: Privately he sees his job as safe for the foreseeable future. He uses AI occasionally for his wife's salon bookings and posts, and he's happy for it to stay at that level.
S0.do: Keeps saving and finally books the family trip to visit Leila's parents. Keeps up mine rescue training and considers taking over as rescue team captain next year.
S0.feel: Calm, with life carrying on as normal.
S0.quote: It can't cut hair, and it can't make people feel looked after, which is what keeps her chairs full.
S0.fieldNote: Diego is steady and family-focused, and his real pride sits with the mine rescue team rather than the shovel. He already uses AI in a practical way for his wife's salon. The plateau changes nothing in his plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is coming and the smart thing is to get ready without panicking. At work I'd tell the crew to keep their eyes open and take any training the company offers. I'd say the company owes us a clear plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, shovels are harder to automate than trucks, but they're working on it. I'd guess the trucks go first, then the shovels become remote-controlled from a room in town. I'd probably end up in that room, but I'd watch for a while before I jumped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see the first remote shovel actually working on our site, then put my name down for the training. Meanwhile I'd keep saving and maybe help Leila open a fourth chair. I'd also push for the mine rescue team to stay staffed by people, because a robot doesn't carry someone out of a smoke-filled tunnel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit of worry in the background, nothing that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why help Leila add a chair now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because her salon is the one thing in our house that robots aren't anywhere near. If the mine gets shaky, I want her side strong. It's maybe ten thousand to set up a chair, and we've got that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you jump into the remote training sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw guys I respect, like Hamid, doing it and liking it. Or if the company tied a pay rise to it. I'm not stubborn, I just don't like being the first to find out something doesn't work.

S1.say: Diego would say change is coming and the smart move is to get ready without panicking. He'd urge the crew to take any training and say the company owes them a clear plan.
S1.think: Privately he expects the trucks to be automated first and shovels to move to remote control from a room in town. He thinks he'd end up in that room but would watch before jumping.
S1.do: Waits for the first remote shovel to work on site, then signs up for training. Spends about ten thousand helping Leila add a fourth chair at the salon and pushes for the mine rescue team to stay staffed by people.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a bit of background worry that doesn't keep him up.
S1.quote: A robot doesn't carry someone out of a smoke-filled tunnel.
S1.fieldNote: Diego is hedging across the household, putting money into his wife's salon because it sits far from automation. His wait-then-move habit is clear and he can name what would speed it up. The mine rescue team is where he draws a line on automation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, and we need the government and companies to work together fast, no point blaming anyone. I'd tell the crew to keep their savings tight and not make big decisions in a panic. I'd stay calm in public because people look to the rescue team guys for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's bad. If robots can do almost anything, the remote shovel room doesn't last either. But Leila's salon would carry on longer than most things, I think, because people still want a person doing their hair. That's what would keep me from losing it completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra chair idea and keep the cash. I'd pay a big chunk off the mortgage straight away. If I lost the job, I'd work in the salon on the business side, the books and bookings, and look for anything practical that robots haven't reached yet, maybe emergency response.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Real pressure, but I'd still feel like I had somewhere to stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people still want a person doing their hair. Are you sure, if robots can do almost anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'm not sure. Maybe a robot could do it perfectly. But I think plenty of people would still pay for Leila, because she knows their kids' names and remembers who's getting married. I could be wrong, but that's what I'd be betting on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mateo, who's about to choose his path?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to hold off on any big loan for university until things settle. Maybe start an apprenticeship that pays from day one. Two years is too fast for anyone to know which jobs are left.

S2.say: Diego would call it a shock and say government and companies must work together fast, without wasting time blaming anyone. He'd keep calm in public and tell the crew to keep savings tight and avoid panic decisions.
S2.think: Privately he thinks it's bad, since even the remote shovel room wouldn't last. He's betting that Leila's salon would carry on longer because people still want a person doing their hair.
S2.do: Drops the extra chair plan, keeps the cash and pays a big chunk off the mortgage straight away. Moves into running the salon's books and bookings if he loses his job, and looks for practical work like emergency response.
S2.feel: Anxious under real pressure, but with a sense of still having somewhere to stand.
S2.quote: She knows their kids' names and remembers who's getting married.
S2.fieldNote: Diego's calm comes from his household having two different legs, the mine and the salon. When pressed, he admitted he isn't sure the salon would be safe, but he'd bet on human contact. His advice to his son is cautious about debt and fast commitments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and we should use it well. I'd want the company to tell us its automation timeline so we can plan. I'd say it at the crew meeting, plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is manageable. I'd get maybe three years on the remote shovel, pay down the house and build up the salon. By the time the end comes, I'd want our household running mostly on Leila's business and our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the remote shovel training once the first few guys came back happy, probably in year one. I'd help Leila add that fourth chair in year two and maybe open a second small salon in the next town by year four. And I'd do a short business course at night, because I'd be the one running the books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The worry is there, but I'd feel like we had a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you dropped the extra chair. Now you'd open a second salon. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time, simply. With two years I want cash in the bank. With five I can try something, see if it works, and still pull back. It's the same as the shovel, you don't dig fast into ground you haven't tested.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truck drivers, honestly. They'll go first, maybe in two years, and some of them are good mates with families. I'd want the company to give them first pick of whatever new jobs there are, even if it's just a year or two of work.

S3.say: Diego would call five years a fair warning that should be used well. He'd want the company to share its automation timeline so the crew can plan.
S3.think: Privately he thinks five years is manageable, with maybe three years on a remote shovel. By the end he wants the household running mostly on Leila's business and their savings.
S3.do: Takes remote shovel training in year one once others confirm it works, and helps Leila add a fourth chair in year two. Plans a second small salon by year four and takes a night course in small business.
S3.feel: Uneasy but steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: You don't dig fast into ground you haven't tested.
S3.fieldNote: Diego explained clearly how more time changes his choices, from holding cash to trying a second salon. His shovel work gives him a natural image for testing before committing. He worries most about the truck drivers, who he expects to go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to plan properly, so there's no excuse for anybody being caught out. I'd want the mines and government to fund retraining, especially for younger workers. I'd keep saying it calmly at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is mostly good for me. I'd be fifty-three with the house paid off and the kids through school, and Leila's business would have had time to grow. The thing I'd worry about is Mateo and Sara, starting careers right as AGI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow the same plan as the five-year one but slower: the remote shovel when it's proven, the business course, maybe the second salon around year five or six. I'd put a bit more into the kids' education savings, but I'd tell them to pick something with people in it. And I'd stay on the rescue team as long as they'll have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly for the kids, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sara, who's eleven now and would be twenty-one in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say find work where people want a human, like nursing, teaching, or Mum's line of work. And learn to use the machines, because whatever she does, they'll be in the room. She wants to be a marine biologist right now, so maybe that works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a moment you'd picture at the end of the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably me in the salon on a Saturday, doing the books, with Leila cutting hair and a robot somewhere out at the pit doing my old job. It sounds strange, but it doesn't sound terrible. I'd miss the shovel, though, the feel of a clean dig.

S4.say: Diego would say ten years is plenty to plan properly, leaving no excuse for anyone being caught out. He'd want the mines and government to fund retraining, especially for younger workers.
S4.think: Privately he thinks ten years is mostly good for him, with the house paid off and Leila's business grown by 53. His real worry is his children starting careers just as AGI arrives.
S4.do: Follows a slower version of the five-year plan, taking remote shovel work when proven and opening a second salon around year five or six. Puts more into the kids' education savings and stays on the rescue team as long as possible.
S4.feel: Uneasy, mostly for his children rather than himself.
S4.quote: It sounds strange, but it doesn't sound terrible. I'd miss the shovel, though, the feel of a clean dig.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Diego's worry shifts almost entirely to his children's futures. His picture of the end point, doing the books in the salon, is calm and specific. He still admits he'd miss the physical skill of the shovel.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's no time to test anything, and testing is how I make decisions. What would help is the companies being honest about their timelines, and help for small businesses like Leila's, because those might be what holds towns together.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The mine rescue team. Everyone talks about jobs, but there's also the stuff we do for each other that nobody pays for. I'd hate to see that disappear because the mine doesn't need people anymore.

headlineQuote: Her salon is the one thing in our house that robots aren't anywhere near.
portrait: Diego Usman is a 43-year-old senior shovel operator at an open-pit gold mine and a proud member of its mine rescue team. His wife Leila owns a three-chair hair salon, and they have two kids, a mortgage and a strong cushion. He's pragmatic and steady, using AI now and then and waiting for proof before he jumps. Across the scenarios he hedges by building up the salon, which he sees as far from automation, and moves to remote shovel work once others test it. The two-year AGI picture makes him anxious because there's no time to test, while the decade picture shifts his worry onto his children.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there's no time to test anything before deciding.
whatWouldHelp: Companies being honest about their automation timelines, and support for small businesses like his wife's salon that hold towns together.
